title: Arteries of the dorsum of the foot (dorsal)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender, with surface detail added by an image model.

rows: Popliteal artery, at the lower border of popliteus.

Passes forward through the opening at the top of the interosseous membrane and runs down on the front of the membrane with the deep fibular nerve, between tibialis anterior and the long extensor muscles of the toes. In front of the ankle joint, midway between the malleoli, it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery.
Muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, with small branches to the knee and ankle joints.
hy: Anterior compartment syndrome: swelling inside the tight anterior compartment, for example after a fracture of the tibia, can cut off the blood flow to its muscles and press on the deep fibular nerve. Severe pain made worse by passive plantarflexion is an early sign. The pulse in the foot is often still present.

rows: Continues the anterior tibial artery in front of the ankle joint, midway between the malleoli.

Runs forward on the dorsum of the foot between the tendons of extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus, with the deep fibular nerve. At the first space between the metatarsals it gives the first dorsal metatarsal artery and dips into the sole as the deep plantar artery, which completes the plantar arch.
Dorsum of the foot and the toes, through its tarsal, arcuate, and dorsal metatarsal branches, and it adds blood to the plantar arch.
hy: Its pulse is felt on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus. A weak or absent pulse suggests peripheral arterial disease, but in some healthy people the artery is small or absent and the pulse cannot be felt.

rows: Dorsalis pedis artery, as it crosses the navicular bone.
Runs laterally across the tarsal bones, under extensor digitorum brevis.
Extensor digitorum brevis and the tarsal bones and joints. It joins the arcuate artery.
Dorsalis pedis artery, near the bases of the metatarsal bones. It is often small or absent.
Runs laterally across the bases of the metatarsal bones, under the tendons of the extensor muscles.
Gives the second, third, and fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries.
The first from the dorsalis pedis artery. The second, third, and fourth usually from the arcuate artery.
Run forward on the dorsal interossei muscles in the spaces between the metatarsal bones. Perforating branches join them to the arteries of the sole.
Each divides into two dorsal digital arteries for the facing sides of two toes.
